title: Deep Water
summary: In this autobiographical account, William O. Douglas describes how a near-drowning in a YMCA swimming pool left him with a crippling fear of water, and how he overcame it through determination and patient training. The experience taught him that fear itself is the real enemy and that conquering it brings a sense of freedom and joy.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: William O. Douglas (1898–1980) was an American judge who served on the US Supreme Court for over thirty-six years, the longest term in its history. The chapter is taken from his autobiography Of Men and Mountains.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: A childhood incident at a California beach first made Douglas wary of water. At ten or eleven, while learning to swim at the YMCA pool, a big bully threw him into the deep end, and he nearly drowned. The terror stayed with him for years, spoiling fishing, canoeing and boating. Finally he hired an instructor who built him into a swimmer bit by bit. He then tested himself in lakes until the fear was gone.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
Early dislike of water. When Douglas was three or four, his father took him to a beach in California, where a wave knocked him down and swept over him. He was frightened, and the memory left a quiet aversion to water.

The YMCA pool. At about ten or eleven he decided to learn swimming at the YMCA pool in Yakima, because it was safer than the river. He used water wings and paddled in the shallow end, still uneasy. One day, while he sat alone at the edge waiting for others, a husky boy of about eighteen picked him up and tossed him into the deep end, laughing.

Near drowning. Douglas swallowed water and sank to the bottom, about nine feet deep. He had planned to spring up from the bottom, but rose slowly and saw only yellowish water. Panic seized him as he tried to scream and could not. He went down a second time, tried again to jump and failed, his legs paralysed. On the third descent, the terror gave way to calm. He felt sleepy, as if he were drifting into peace, and then lost consciousness. He woke up lying beside the pool, vomiting, with the bully and others around him.

The haunting fear. For years the fear of water ruined his holidays. Whenever he waded into lakes or went canoeing, the terror returned and his legs felt paralysed. In October he decided to fight it.

Training with an instructor. He hired an instructor who, for three months, trained him five days a week, an hour each day. A rope attached to a belt around his waist ran through a pulley overhead so the instructor could hold him. First he learnt to put his face under water and breathe out, then to kick with his legs, then to move his arms. Piece by piece, he became a swimmer. The instructor’s work was done by April, but traces of terror remained, so Douglas swam alone in the pool, lengths after lengths, ordering the fear away whenever it rose.

Final test. In July he went to Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire, dived off a dock at Triggs Island and swam two miles across the lake. Later he swam in Warm Lake and climbed Gilbert Peak, looking down on Conrad Meadows. The fear had left him. He understood that in death there is peace and that the fear of death is worse than death itself. He would recall the sentence of a US President that the only thing to fear is fear.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Overcoming fear: courage is not the absence of fear but the will to face it.
  • Determination and perseverance: patient practice over months turns weakness into strength.
  • The will to live: the urge to survive drives the struggle in the pool.
  • Freedom through self-mastery: conquering fear released him to enjoy life fully.

notes.heading: Character sketch
notes.html:
Douglas: a sensitive child who becomes a resolute adult. He is honest about his panic, analytical about his fear, and methodical in conquering it. Hiring an instructor shows humility; swimming alone till the last trace of terror disappeared shows grit. His reflection on death and fear shows philosophical depth.

The instructor: patient and skilful, he builds the swimmer stage by stage using a rope and pulley so that Douglas gains confidence without risk.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: ‘Deep Water’ refers both to the deep end of the YMCA pool where Douglas nearly drowned and, symbolically, to the deep fear that submerged him for years. The title captures the danger and the depth of the struggle.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Fear grows when we avoid it and shrinks when we face it step by step. With determination, patience and the right guidance, any phobia can be overcome, and the freedom gained is worth the effort.

keyTerms.definition: A strong dislike; Douglas’s early aversion to water began at the California beach.
Inflatable armbands that keep a learner afloat.
A big, strong, aggressive person; the eighteen-year-old who threw Douglas into the pool.
An intense, irrational fear; Douglas’s hydrophobia (fear of water).
Unable to move; how Douglas’s legs felt each time terror returned.
A wheel with a rope used by the instructor to hold Douglas during training.
The traces of fear that remained after training, which Douglas removed by swimming alone.
A first-person account of the writer’s own life experience.

mcqs.q: How old was Douglas when a wave knocked him down at the beach?
mcqs.explanation: The beach incident in California happened when he was three or four years old.

mcqs.q: Why did Douglas choose the YMCA pool to learn swimming?
options: It was safe compared to the Yakima River.
mcqs.explanation: His mother thought the river was treacherous, so the pool was considered safe.

mcqs.q: Who threw Douglas into the deep end of the pool?
options: A big bruiser of about eighteen
mcqs.explanation: A husky eighteen-year-old boy tossed him in for fun.

mcqs.q: What was Douglas’s plan when he first sank to the bottom?
options: To jump up from the bottom and reach the surface
mcqs.explanation: He planned to spring up from the bottom and come up like a cork, but it did not work.

mcqs.q: What did Douglas feel when he went down for the third time?
options: Calm and peace, as terror stopped
mcqs.explanation: On the third descent the terror ended; he felt sleepy and peaceful before blacking out.

mcqs.q: How did the instructor ensure Douglas’s safety during training?
options: By staying in the water with him
By a rope attached to a belt and running through a pulley
By letting him swim only in shallow water
mcqs.explanation: A rope through an overhead pulley attached to Douglas’s belt let the instructor hold him up.

mcqs.q: In what order did the instructor train Douglas?
mcqs.explanation: First exhaling under water, then kicking with legs, then arm strokes, building a swimmer piece by piece.

mcqs.q: Where did Douglas swim two miles to test himself?
mcqs.explanation: He swam across Lake Wentworth in New Hampshire, from Triggs Island.

mcqs.q: What did Douglas conclude about death and fear?
options: The fear of death is worse than death itself.
mcqs.explanation: He realised there is peace in death and that only the fear of death is to be feared.

mcqs.q: Why did Douglas continue swimming alone after the instructor’s training ended?
options: He was not fully sure the terror was gone and wanted to remove its traces.
He wanted to win a race.
mcqs.explanation: Some residual terror remained, so he swam alone, challenging the fear whenever it appeared.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Douglas describes how, while sinking for the second time, he tried to jump up from the bottom but his legs would not obey him, and he felt utterly helpless.
(a) What had he planned to do on reaching the bottom? (1)
(b) Why did the plan fail? (1)
(c) Which emotion dominated him at this point? (1)
(d) Give a word from the chapter meaning ‘unable to move’. (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) He had planned to spring up from the bottom and rise to the surface.

(b) Terror had gripped him and his legs were too stiff and weak to push off.

(c) Sheer panic and helplessness.

(d) Paralysed.

questions.q: How did the experience at the YMCA pool affect Douglas’s life?
questions.answerHtml: The near drowning left a deep fear of water that haunted him for years. He could not enjoy canoeing, boating, fishing or swimming in lakes, because whenever he entered water his legs felt paralysed and the old terror returned, spoiling his holidays.

questions.q: What did Douglas do to get over his fear of water?
questions.answerHtml: He hired an instructor who trained him for three months using a rope and pulley. He learnt to breathe out under water, kick with his legs and stroke with his arms. Then he swam alone in the pool and later across lakes until the fear vanished.

questions.q: Why does Douglas say that ‘all we have to fear is fear itself’ applied to him?
questions.answerHtml: Douglas had experienced both death’s approach and the fear of it. He found the actual moment of drowning peaceful, while the fear afterwards crippled him for years. So it was the fear, not the water, that was his real enemy, and conquering it freed him.

questions.q: Describe Douglas’s experience of nearly drowning in the YMCA pool. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Douglas was about ten or eleven and still nervous in water when an eighteen-year-old bully picked him up and flung him into the nine-foot deep end of the YMCA pool. He swallowed water and sank. Though frightened, he had a plan: he would spring up from the bottom and rise to the surface. But he rose slowly, his eyes open to nothing but yellow water, and panic seized him. He tried to shout but no sound came.

He sank a second time and again tried to jump, but his legs were paralysed by fear. Desperate, he reached for something solid but there was only water. On the third descent, the terror suddenly gave way to calm. He felt drowsy and peaceful, as if drifting into sleep, and lost consciousness. He woke up beside the pool, vomiting. The incident left a fear that dominated his life for years.

questions.q: ‘Deep Water’ is a story of courage and determination. Discuss. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
‘Deep Water’ shows how courage and determination can defeat even a deep-rooted fear. After almost drowning as a boy, Douglas lived with a terror of water that spoiled his holidays and denied him the pleasures of lakes and rivers. Instead of accepting it, he decided to fight.

He hired an instructor and trained patiently for three months, an hour a day, five days a week. He learnt each skill separately: breathing out under water, kicking, then using his arms. When the training ended and slight fear remained, he did not give up. He swam alone, length after length, scolding the terror away whenever it rose.

Finally he tested himself by swimming two miles across Lake Wentworth and later in Warm Lake, emerging triumphant. His journey proves that courage means facing fear repeatedly. Through willpower and perseverance he not only learnt to swim but gained a lasting sense of freedom and confidence.
